newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Rugby League-Super League clears final legal hurdle.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Rugby League-Super League clears final legal hurdle.

text.p: Media baron Rupert Murdoch's breakaway Super League won a final and decisive court victory on Friday, defeating the last remaining legal threat to its scheduled kick-off in Australia next year.
The country's high court denied the Australian Rugby League (ARL), Murdoch's rival in the battle for control of the sport, leave to appeal an earlier ruling which freed Super Legaue to start in 1997.
The court ruling ends an 14-month legal tussle and means the 10-team Super League will run in direct competition with the 12 teams in the existing ARL premiership next season.
"This welcome decision vindicates the earlier findings and puts an end to the legal battle over rugby league," a Super League spokeswoman said.
"We can now get on with starting a new competition. Super League will announce its fixture list for the 1997 season next Wednesday," she added.
ARL chairman Ken Arthurson said the eventual winner of rugby league's civil war in Australia would now be decided by the quality of the rival competitions.
"The good news is that the arguments are now confined to the football field," Arthurson said.
After a hearing lasting one hour on Friday, the three high court judges adjourned for 15 minutes before ruling there were no new grounds to warrant an appeal.
The ARL application was opposed by the Super league-aligned Brisbane Broncos club, a group of more than 300 players, and News Ltd, the Australian arm of Murdoch's global media empire.

The federal court last month ruled that five-year loyalty agreements between the ARL and 20 clubs breached trade practices legislation, overturning an earlier court decision and freeing eight rebel clubs to play under the Super League banner.
The legal battle between News Ltd and the ARL began in September 1995 when Murdoch challenged the legality of the loyalty agreements, signed in February 1995.
